notes.1a: Candidates generally gave the correct number of paperbacks, although 250 and 1000 were seen.
notes.1b: Most candidates found the number of non-fiction books correctly.
notes.1c: This part was generally correct, although equivalent fractions such as 33/275 were seen.
notes.1d: This part was generally well answered. However, subtracting 14% rather than adding was seen.
notes.1e: Many candidates found this part difficult and assumed 10 dollars had to be subtracted or 5 dollars added.
notes.1f: This part was generally well answered, although common errors of 35 × 103 and 3.5 × 10-4 were seen Answers: (a) 1750 (b) 660 (c) 3/25, (d) 3135 (e) 9475 (f) 3.5 × 104
notes.2a: (i) Although generally correct, occasionally marks were lost in this part for giving one inaccurate value.
notes.2aii: This part was generally correct, with 28 and 84 often seen. However, some candidates did not understand that the numbers had to be a common multiple of both 4 and 7.
notes.2b: (i) This part was generally well answered, although 16 was a common error.
notes.2bii: Many candidates did not understand the need to use the two concepts of prime and square.
notes.2d: This was the least successful part of the question. Candidates sometimes ignored the fact that k and m should be prime and tried to find any two numbers (sometimes decimal numbers) which would satisfy the equation. Answers: (a)(i) any five multiples of 7 (a)(ii) two multiples of 28 (b)(i) 25 (b)(ii) 17
notes.3: The plotting and drawing in this question was of a good standard.
notes.3a: The majority of candidates were able to complete the table successfully and to score full marks.
notes.3b: The plotting of points and the drawing of the curve was generally good, with few straight line segments seen.
notes.3c: This was less successfully answered with a significant number of candidates offering no answer or giving the intersections with the x-axis rather than y = 2.
notes.3dii: Most candidates drew the correct line on the grid.
notes.3iii: This part was less successfully answered; many candidates tried to read the gradient from the graph but used the number of squares rather than the values to determine the rise over the length.
notes.3e: The coordinates of intersection of the two graphs was generally given correctly. Answers: (a) 3, 5, -1 (b) correct curve drawn (c) their curve’s intercept with y = 2
notes.4a: Many correct answers were seen here. The main errors were to incorrectly multiply out brackets (for example to write 3x+1) or subtracting a coefficient of x rather than dividing by it.
notes.4b: Many correct rearrangements were seen in this part. Common errors were an answer of (g+7)/5 or an initial wrong first step such as g – 5 = 7f.
notes.4c: Although many candidates scored full marks in this part, there were a number who had only one of 2 or y as a common factor. Answers: (a) 7.5 (b) (g+5)/7 (c) 2y(3x-5z)
notes.5: In this question on trigonometry, some candidates lost method marks for not showing any working.
notes.5a: Very few candidates gave the correct answer here. The most common incorrect answers given were similar, same, equal or no answer given.
notes.5b: Many candidates understood the calculation required. However, some did not use the trigonometric functions correctly. A common error seen was tanDBC = 11/8.
notes.5c: (i) The majority of candidates understood they needed to use ½ × base × height. A common error was to use the incorrect value of x and write ½ × 8 × 11.
notes.5cii: Many candidates understood that the total area was twice that of the triangle so gained the mark.
notes.5d: Candidates did not appear to understand how to formulate the necessary equation as a considerable minority did not attempt this part. Those that did attempt it and wrote down a linear equation were usually able to simplify it. Answers: (a) congruent (b) 36.0o (c)(i) 20 (c)(ii) 40 (d) 14 �PAGE�36
notes.6: This question involved constructions and most candidates made a good attempt. There was a lack of clear construction arcs and misreading of angles which caused some candidates to lose marks.
notes.6a: The vast majority of candidates were able to construct the triangle. In a few cases the lengths of AC and BC were interchanged.
notes.6b: Many candidates measured the angle correctly. A common error was to measure one of the other two angles in the triangle or the supplementary angle.
notes.6c: (i) This construction was poorly attempted by many candidates even though they understood the requirements to bisect an angle. The main error was inaccuracy.
notes.6cii: This construction was also poorly attempted. Besides inaccuracies, the other common error was to create a perpendicular where the angle bisector crossed AC. In this part some candidates misread the question and created a ‘correct’ perpendicular bisector of another side of the triangle.
notes.6d: (i) 0.7 to 0.8 cm (d)(ii) region of triangle between their constructions (e) 500
notes.6dii: This part was very poorly answered. Candidates did not generally understand which region had to be shaded. Some candidates who did understand, lost the mark because they did not completely shade the area, stopping at a construction arc instead.
notes.6e: The majority of candidates understood how to use the scale but missed the fact that there was a need to make the units the same. Consequently 5 was the most common answer. Answers: (a) correct triangle drawn (b) 46o (c)(i) correct angle bisector drawn with construction arcs (c)(ii) correct perpendicular bisector drawn with construction arcs
notes.7: The concept of sequences was well understood by the vast majority of candidates. Working out the value of lower position terms in a sequence was seen as straightforward. However, the ability to determine and use nth term formulae was poor.
notes.7a: (i), (ii), (iii) Most candidates wrote the next term and the 8th term correctly, but found the nth term more difficult, often writing n+4.
notes.7b: (i) Very well answered with nearly all candidates gaining the mark.
notes.7bii: Although many candidates obtained the correct answer, a similar number gave an answer of 2 with no working.
notes.7iii: Surprisingly many candidates did not use their value from (b)(ii) in the formula to gain an answer. Answers: (a)(i) 21 (a)(ii) 33 (a)(iii) 4n+1 (b)(i) 40 (b)(ii) 3 (b)(iii) 10300 �PAGE�37
notes.8: Candidates appeared to understand the general concept of calculating probabilities well but were less clear about converting a probability into the number of cars. An error amongst some candidates was to assume the total contained just the red and blue cars, i.e. 29 instead of 50 cars.
notes.8a: (i) Many candidates gave the correct probability that the car was red.
notes.8aii: Many candidates also gave the correct probability that the car was red or blue.
notes.8iii: This was less well attempted; some candidates assumed that not blue was equivalent to red so gave the same answer as (a)(i).
notes.8iv: The majority of candidates understood that no yellow cars was equivalent to a zero probability.
notes.8b: This part was less successfully answered, with an answer of 1/50 often given. Answers: (a)(i) 19/50 (a)(ii) 29/50 (a)(iii) 40/50 (a)(iv) 0 (b) 50
notes.9a: The majority of candidates were able to gain full marks in this part. The common error was to give the total number of visitors, 469, and not divide by 7 to give the average.
notes.9b: This part was not attempted as well as part (a). The concept of range did not appear to be fully understood. Common errors were to quote the range as 34-96 or to state either the maximum or minimum value.
notes.9c: The bar chart was generally well attempted, but marks were lost for inaccurate plotting and not labelling the axes. Answers: (a) 67 (b) 62 (c) correct labelled vertical scale and correct bar chart
notes.10: Candidates lost marks in this question for not giving their answers to two decimal places as stated in the question. Marks were also lost because some candidates interchanged the formulae for simple and compound interest.
notes.10a: (i) The change from dollars to euros was generally well done. A common error was to divide by 0.6513 instead of multiplying by it.
notes.10aii: The change from euros to dollars was similarly well done. A common error was to multiply by 0.6513 instead of dividing by it.
notes.10b: For those candidates that attempted simple interest, the main error was to not include the zero as the second decimal place.
notes.10c: If candidates used the method of calculating the interest for one year, adding it to the original amount to give 583.00 and then repeating for the second year, many went on to give just the interest in the final year or added together 583.00 and 617.98. Answers: (a)(i) 325.65 (a)(ii) 460.61 or 460.62 (b) 349.70 (c) 617.98 �PAGE�38
notes.11: This question showed a generally good understanding and appreciation of transformations with the majority of candidates able to attempt a description of the given transformations and able to attempt to draw a translation and enlargement.
notes.11a: (i) Many candidates gave the correct transformation. A common error was to give the line of reflection as x = 0 instead of the x-axis.
notes.11aii: Candidates tended to omit one of the three necessary parts of the transformation, usually the centre of rotation. Some candidates gave the answer as two transformations.
notes.11bii: Drawing an enlargement proved more difficult than the previous part. The common error seen was to enlarge about a wrong centre of enlargement. Answers: (a)(i) reflection in the x-axis (a)(ii) rotation about the origin, 90o
notes.general_comments:
This paper gave the opportunity for candidates to demonstrate their knowledge and application of
Mathematics. The majority of the candidates were able to use the allocated time to good effect and
complete the paper. The majority of candidates answered all of the questions with some omitting a few part
questions. The standard of presentation and amount of working shown was generally good apart from
showing all construction lines in Question 6. Centres should continue to encourage candidates to show
clear working in the answer space provided, and show the formulae used, substitutions and calculations
performed.
